segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, found?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For what does the Scripture say?

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now to the one who works, the wages are not counted as a matter of grace but as a matter of debt.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But to the one who does not work, but believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as David also pronounces the blessing on the person to whom God counts righteousness apart from works:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: blessed is the man against whom the Lord will never count sin.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Is this blessing, then, on the circumcised, or also on the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: How then was it counted? When he was circumcised or uncircumcised? Not when he was circumcised, but when he was uncircumcised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while uncircumcised, so that he would be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the father of the circumcised, for those who are not merely circumcised but also follow in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring, that he would be heir of the world, did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise has been nullified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the law produces wrath; but where there is no law, there is no transgression either.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason it is by faith, so that it may be a matter of grace, in order that the promise may be secure for all the offspring, not only for those who are of the law but also for those who are of the faith of Abraham. He is the father of us all,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I have made you the father of many nations.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He is our father in the presence of the God whom he believed, the one who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they were.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Against hope, in hope he believed, and so became the father of many nations, according to what had been said:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “So shall your offspring be.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And without weakening in faith, he considered his own body, as good as dead since he was about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah’s womb,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: yet with regard to the promise of God he did not waver in unbelief but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and being fully convinced that what God had promised, he was also able to do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “it was counted to him as righteousness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the words

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “it was counted to him”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: were not written for his sake alone,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but also for our sake. It is going to be counted to us who believe in the one who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who was handed over for our offenses and raised for our justification.

notes.traditional: What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has found?
notes.note: The Greek can also be punctuated as two questions: “What then shall we say? Have we found Abraham to be our forefather according to the flesh?” On that reading Paul is asking whether physical descent is what makes Abraham “our” father. Most translations take it as here. Manuscripts also differ on where the word “found” stands, and a few omit it.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: “justify,” “just” and “justice” on one side, “righteous” and “righteousness” on the other. “Justified” here and “righteousness” in verse 3 are therefore the same root, and to be justified is to be declared or set in the right. Some scholars prefer “justice” or “covenant faithfulness” for the noun.

The verb is a bookkeeping term for entering something to a person’s account, and Paul uses it eleven times in this chapter. It is rendered “count” throughout so that the repetition is visible, including in verse 4 (wages) and verse 8 (sin). Other versions use “credited,” “reckoned” or “imputed.”

Most modern versions have “as a gift” or “as a favor” here. The Greek phrase is identical to the one in verse 16, and the word is Paul’s usual term for grace, so both verses are rendered alike to keep the link: wages are owed, but what God gives rests on grace.

notes.phrase: those who are not merely circumcised but also follow in the footsteps
notes.note: The Greek repeats the article in a way that, read strictly, would name two groups: the circumcised, and those who follow Abraham’s faith. Most interpreters judge the extra article a slip or a loose construction and understand one group, Jews who also share Abraham’s faith, as translated here.

The Greek word here is the same one translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in Romans (for example 3:29). In the quotation from Genesis 17:5 it means peoples in general, but Paul’s readers would have heard in it that Abraham is the father of Gentile believers as well as Jewish ones.

notes.phrase: calls the things that are not as though they were
notes.traditional: calls into existence the things that do not exist
notes.note: The Greek is literally “calling the things not being as being.” Many translations take this as God’s creative call that brings things into existence. The rendering here follows the more direct sense of the grammar: God speaks of what does not yet exist, such as Abraham’s many descendants, as already real. Both readings have strong scholarly support.

The Greek construction can express result (“and so he became”), purpose (“in order to become”) or the content of what Abraham believed (“believed that he would become”). The result reading is adopted here; the others are grammatically possible, and translations are divided.

Many later manuscripts read “he did not consider his own body,” which the King James Version follows; the earliest witnesses lack the negative. With the negative, Abraham’s faith ignored the obstacles; without it, he faced them squarely and still believed. Some manuscripts also add “already” before “as good as dead.”

The traditional “delivered” or “delivered up” is now unclear English. The verb is the ordinary word for handing someone into another’s power, and the Gospels use it for each stage of Jesus’ arrest and execution. The passive leaves the agent unstated, and the wording probably echoes Isaiah 53 in the Greek Old Testament.

The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. “Trespass,” the rendering of the Tyndale and King James tradition and of several modern versions, now mainly suggests entering property without permission. “Offense” is a standard gloss for the word, and its meaning is not disputed.

The same Greek preposition stands in both halves of the verse and normally means “because of.” The first half is naturally “because of our offenses.” The second is debated: either “because we had been justified” or, as most hold, “with a view to our justification.” “For” is used twice to keep the parallel and leave the question open.

Recurs throughout the New Testament with versions shifting between grace, favor, gift and thanks; the line between “grace” and “gift/favor” needs a single ruling.
Abraham’s “seed/offspring/descendants” is a thread through Romans, Galatians, Hebrews, Luke and John, and Galatians 3:16 turns on the singular, so one rendering is needed.
Occurs across Paul and John with senses from physical descent to sinful nature; translators diverge widely and consistency of “according to the flesh” matters.
